1093.title: Calling Sri Near
1093.hook: Diwali night, the door left open, and a hymn that calls the goddess near and hopes she is glad to come
1093.carry: puja: welcoming the divine as a beloved guest
1093.tomorrow: why do coins pour from Lakshmi's hand?
1093.howItsDone: In Lakshmi worship at home, some families clean the house and light lamps before reciting the Sri Sukta, especially at Diwali, as a way of welcoming the goddess.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday asked for the Lakshmi who does not go away: Lakshmi stays where she is honored. Today, the hymn hears her coming.
screen: `THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.`

segments.voice: You hear a wedding procession before you see it. Drums from two streets over. Then horns, then a crowd, then the horse with the groom on it, swaying, decorated, a little embarrassed. Everyone on the block comes to the window. Something important is arriving, and it's loud about it. The next line of the Sri Sukta sounds like that. The singer hears the goddess coming before she's in the room. And when she gets there, he doesn't ask for anything yet. He asks one thing about her.
screen: `DRUMS FROM TWO STREETS OVER.` → `EVERYONE COMES TO THE WINDOW.` → `SOMETHING IMPORTANT ARRIVING.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Horses go before her, a chariot carries her in the middle, and she delights in the trumpeting of elephants. I call the goddess Sri near. May the goddess Sri be pleased with me. Royalty arriving: Sri comes the way a queen comes into a city, and the whole street knows. Then the verb. I call her near. The singer is still at the door, inviting. And then the request, quieter than you'd expect. Not give me. Not bless me. May she be pleased with me. The Sanskrit word carries the sense of taking pleasure in, being glad of. That changes the shape of the whole hymn. It isn't a vending machine, coins in and fortune out. It's hosting someone you love and hoping they feel at home. And that is the heart of how Hindus worship. A puja is hospitality. The deity is offered a seat, water for the feet, flowers, a lamp, food, the welcome you'd give an honored guest in your home. You can't order a guest to be happy. You can sweep the floor, light the lamp, and hope. That's why, on Diwali night, many families leave the lamps burning and the door open: Lakshmi is being invited in. Notice the name, too. Sri is the honor people put before other names, on a letter or a wedding card. In this hymn it's the goddess herself: radiance, beauty, good fortune, all in one word.
screen: `HORSES, A CHARIOT, ELEPHANTS.` · `I CALL HER NEAR.` · `MAY SHE BE PLEASED WITH ME.` · `A PUJA IS HOSPITALITY.` · then, large: `HOSTING, NOT ORDERING.`

segments.voice: Light a lamp or a candle if you can, the way families do for Lakshmi, or picture one burning by your door. Notice what a welcome would look like here: one thing straightened, one light on. Then sit inside that welcome as if someone you love were on the way. If you pray, you can call the goddess, or God, near in your own words and offer the light; if you don't, let the lit room be a welcome for whatever good you hope will come.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn that hears Sri coming, with horses, a chariot and elephants, and asks only that she be pleased to be here.

segments.voice: Your line: puja is welcoming the divine as a beloved guest. A guest can't be ordered to be happy, only welcomed. See you tomorrow.

1094.title: Satisfied and Satisfying
1094.hook: a cook who eats last and fills every plate, and a goddess whose open hand pours coins
1094.carry: lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward
1094.tomorrow: why do some Hindus go to Lakshmi first?
1094.howItsDone: Images of Lakshmi in homes and temples often show her seated or standing on a lotus, and the Sri Sukta's descriptions of her are chanted in front of such images during Lakshmi worship.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hymn heard her coming, horses, a chariot, elephants, and asked only that she be pleased to be here: puja, welcoming the divine as a beloved guest.
screen: `MAY SHE BE PLEASED WITH ME.`

segments.voice: At a big family dinner there's often one person who eats last. She's been at the stove since noon. She notices your plate is empty before you do, and fills it, and fills the next one. And when she finally sits down, she doesn't look tired so much as content, the way someone looks when they had enough to give. The Sri Sukta has a phrase for that. Today the hymn stops calling the goddess and starts describing her, and one pair of words sits right in the middle.
screen: `SHE EATS LAST.` → `SHE FILLS EVERY PLATE.` → `CONTENT, NOT TIRED.`

segments.voice: First, where she comes from. The Puranas tell that when the gods and the demons churned the ocean of milk, treasures rose out of it one by one, and then Lakshmi rose, seated on a lotus, and the whole world brightened. The Sri Sukta paints her in that light. Here's the line, in paraphrase. Smiling, within a wall of gold, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying, standing on the lotus, the color of the lotus: I call Sri near. Start with the strange pairing: moist and blazing. Wet and on fire at once. Some readers hear tenderness and radiance; others, the monsoon and the sun a field needs. The hymn lets her hold both. Then the pair this day is about: satisfied, and satisfying. In Sanskrit the two words echo, triptam tarpayantim. She is full, and she makes others full. Notice the order. Her fullness comes first, and the filling flows out of it. That's the cook at the dinner table: she isn't giving from an empty pot. And here's the teaching families see every Diwali. In so many pictures of Lakshmi, gold coins pour from her open hand. Her wealth isn't locked behind the gold wall; it spills. Many Hindus take that as how fortune should move through a home: what comes in goes out again, as sweets carried to the neighbors, gifts, and giving to people in need. A goddess of wealth who hoards wouldn't be Lakshmi. She's smiling, soft and bright. She has enough, and so she shares.
screen: `SHE ROSE FROM THE OCEAN OF MILK.` · `MOIST AND BLAZING AT ONCE.` · `SATISFIED, AND SATISFYING.` · `COINS POUR FROM HER HAND.` · then, large: `FULL, AND SO SHE FILLS.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come in all the way, without forcing it, and go out slowly, as if you're giving it away: in until you're full, out as a gift. If a face comes to mind, someone who could use a little of what you have, let them sit with you on the out-breath, and choose one small thing to share with them this week: a sweet, a call, a little money. If you pray, you can offer them to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, just keep breathing in and giving out.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that paints Sri smiling, moist and blazing, standing on the lotus: satisfied, and satisfying.
screen: `THE SRI SUKTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward. Full first, and then the filling flows. Until tomorrow.

1095.title: I Choose You
1095.hook: Lakshmi choosing Vishnu from the ocean of milk, and the line where the hymn stops saying 'her' and says 'you'
1095.carry: prapatti: taking refuge is a choice
1095.tomorrow: why is the fortune goddess's tree so hard to crack?
1095.howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Sri Sukta in full during Lakshmi worship at home or in temples, so this verse of refuge is spoken as part of the whole hymn.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday painted her portrait: smiling, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying. Lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward.
screen: `SATISFIED, AND SATISFYING.`

segments.voice: A cover letter begins: to whom it may concern. Polite, careful, written to a title. Three paragraphs later, if the job matters enough, it starts to sound like a person talking to a person. A speech at a retirement party can go the same way: it starts about the colleague, and ends turned toward her, glass up, speaking to her directly. Something like that happens in the Sri Sukta today. For several lines the singer has talked about the goddess. Called her near. Described her. Then, at the end of one line, the pronoun changes.
screen: `TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN.` → `A PERSON TALKING TO A PERSON.` → `THE PRONOUN CHANGES.`

segments.voice: A story first. The Bhagavata Purana tells that when Lakshmi rose from the churned ocean, she looked over the gods, sages and demons, found a flaw in each, and chose Vishnu, placing her garland on him. She chose. Today the Sri Sukta turns that around. Here's the line, in paraphrase. Bright as the moon, blazing with glory, Sri, cherished by the gods, generous: I take refuge in her, the lotus one. May misfortune be gone from me. I choose you. The first half is still the portrait. Then a step closer. I take refuge in her. Refuge is what you look for when you've run out of ways to manage on your own. The singer isn't only admiring her now; he's placing himself under her shelter. Then the request: may misfortune be gone. The word is Alakshmi, and she'll come back with a face of her own. And then the last two words. Tvam vrine. I choose you. All along it's been she, her, Sri. Suddenly it's you. The singer turns and speaks to her face to face. She chose once; now he chooses her. Here is the teaching. His words for refuge, sharanam prapadye, gave Hindus a name for a whole path: prapatti, surrender, taking refuge in God. In the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India, devotees take refuge in Vishnu through Sri, honored as the mother who brings them in. Surrender, in this tradition, isn't giving up. It's choosing whom to turn to.
screen: `SHE CHOSE VISHNU.` · `I TAKE REFUGE IN HER.` · `MAY MISFORTUNE BE GONE.` · `PRAPATTI, TAKING REFUGE.` · then, large: `I CHOOSE YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that's been weighing on you, a stretch of bad luck or a worry you keep circling, and let it be there. Then turn toward your shelter the way the hymn turns from her to you. If you pray, you can say the old words of refuge in your own language, 'I take refuge in you,' to the goddess, or to God, and rest there; if you don't, ask yourself gently where you go for shelter, a person, a place, a practice, and rest under it.

1096.title: Born of Her Tapas
1096.hook: a fruit with a shell you need a hammer for, a grandmother's Friday fast, and a tree born from the goddess's discipline
1096.carry: tapas: even fortune grows from disciplined heat
1096.tomorrow: who is Alakshmi, and why do families scrub before Diwali?
1096.howItsDone: The bilva tree is treated as sacred in Hindu worship, where its leaves are offered, and this verse is recited as part of the Sri Sukta in Lakshmi worship.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday turned to her directly: I take refuge, I choose you. Prapatti: taking refuge is a choice. Today, a tree.
screen: `I CHOOSE YOU.`

segments.voice: The bilva fruit does not look generous. It's round and greenish-gold, with a shell so hard that people crack it against a stone step or with the back of a cleaver. Inside is a sticky, fragrant pulp that some families stir into a cool summer drink. It's the same tree whose leaves this path saw offered to Shiva. You might expect a softer fruit for a goddess of abundance, a mango, maybe. But when the Sri Sukta names her tree, it names this one. And it says where the tree came from.
screen: `A SHELL YOU NEED A HAMMER FOR.` → `FRAGRANT PULP INSIDE.` → `HER TREE IS THE BILVA.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. O you who are the color of the sun, from your tapas the lord of the forest was born: your tree, the bilva. May its fruits, by tapas, drive away the misfortunes within and without. Start with tapas. It means heat, and then the heat of discipline: effort, austerity, the steady fire of a hard practice. In the old stories, sages keep that fire burning in the forest, and gods win their boons with it. And here's the surprise: the hymn gives tapas to Sri. The goddess of fortune, gold and ease is the one whose discipline makes the tree grow. In this line, abundance isn't the opposite of effort. It comes out of it. Then the tree. Lord of the forest is an old way of saying a great tree, and its fruits push away misfortune by tapas too. The outer misfortunes are easy to list: an empty purse, a roof that leaks. The inner ones are harder; some readers hear confusion there, the habits that block a person from within. Now the teaching, because Hindus live it. Tapas runs all through the faith, even in Lakshmi's worship. Many families keep a vrat for her, a vow: a Friday fast, since Friday is her day, or in the South the Varalakshmi vow, a day of fasting and worship for the goddess. A small heat, kept on purpose, in the name of the one whose own tapas grew a tree.
screen: `THE COLOR OF THE SUN.` · `TAPAS, THE HEAT OF DISCIPLINE.` · `HER TREE, THE BILVA.` · `A FRIDAY VOW FOR LAKSHMI.` · then, large: `ABUNDANCE GROWN FROM EFFORT.`

segments.voice: Choose to stay still, really still, for the whole sit, even when something itches or the mind wants to wander: that's tapas at its smallest, staying a little longer than is comfortable. When the mind wanders, bring it back; the bringing back is the practice. If you keep a fast or a vow, remember it now. If you pray, you can offer the effort to the goddess, or to God; if you don't, let the stillness be its own offering.
The Sri Sukta. A hymn that says the bilva tree was born from the goddess's own tapas, and asks its fruit to drive away misfortune within and without.

segments.voice: Your line: tapas, even fortune grows from disciplined heat. Her own tapas grew the bilva tree. See you tomorrow.

1097.title: Alakshmi Out, Lakshmi In
1097.hook: a stove scrubbed at 10pm before Diwali, and a hymn that gives misfortune a face and shows it the door
1097.tomorrow: is Lakshmi only the goddess of money?
1097.howItsDone: Some Hindu households clean the house thoroughly before Diwali and Lakshmi worship, and some describe it as clearing Alakshmi out before welcoming Lakshmi in.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-SEVEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday named her tree, the bilva, born from her own tapas: even fortune grows from disciplined heat. Today, the hymn meets the one it wants gone.
screen: `THE BILVA, BORN OF HER TAPAS.`

segments.voice: A home can have a corner that sags. The junk drawer that won't close. The sink that's been full since Tuesday. The pile of mail nobody wants to open. None of it is a disaster. But walk into a room like that when you're already tired, and something heavy can settle on the shoulders. The Sri Sukta has a name for that heaviness, and it isn't shy about it. A few lines ago the singer asked for misfortune to be gone. Today the hymn describes her, and then rolls up its sleeves.
screen: `THE DRAWER THAT WON'T CLOSE.` → `THE SINK FULL SINCE TUESDAY.` → `A NAME FOR THE HEAVINESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Hunger and thirst and grime, the elder one, Alakshmi: I drive her away. Non-prosperity, lack, all of it, push it out of my house. Alakshmi is the hymn's word for misfortune, the shadow of Lakshmi. And look at what she's made of. Not curses or monsters. Hunger. Thirst. Dirt. The ordinary signs of a house that's struggling. Then the word elder. In later tellings, tradition makes Alakshmi Lakshmi's older sister, and some honor her as a goddess in her own right, as Jyeshtha, the elder. The hymn itself just gives the word and moves on. Now the grammar, because it's the surprise. The first verb is I. I drive her away. For once, the singer isn't only asking; he takes part. Then he turns back to the goddess: you, push the rest out of my house. Many teachers read a partnership in that: the person sweeps, and grace finishes the work. And here is a big reason Hindu families clean so hard before Diwali. Scrubbing, whitewashing, throwing out what's broken. Many say it plainly: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in. In parts of Bengal, families even see a small figure of Alakshmi out of the house before Lakshmi is worshipped. Fortune in this hymn lives in a household, and a household has dishes and floors and a pantry to keep. Misfortune here isn't a fate from the sky. It has a face and an address, and the family is willing to show it the door, before the lamps are lit and the guest comes in.
screen: `HUNGER, THIRST AND GRIME.` · `ALAKSHMI, THE ELDER ONE.` · `I DRIVE HER AWAY; YOU FINISH IT.` · `WHY FAMILIES SCRUB BEFORE DIWALI.` · then, large: `ALAKSHMI OUT, LAKSHMI IN.`

segments.voice: In your mind, find the corner of your home that sags, the drawer, the sink, the pile, and look at it honestly, without scolding yourself. Then picture it clear, one surface empty and wiped, and breathe there; after this, clear it for real, the way families do before Diwali. 1098.title: Rich in Cattle, Rich in Truth
1098.hook: a cowshed at dawn, jasmine on the door, eight Lakshmis, and a hymn that counts truth of speech as riches
1098.tomorrow: why does Lakshmi always sit on a lotus?
1098.howItsDone: In some Hindu homes, especially in villages, cattle are honored at festivals and floors and courtyards are freshly plastered and decorated before Lakshmi worship; the Sri Sukta is chanted as part of that worship.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday gave misfortune a face, Alakshmi, and the singer helped show her the door: Alakshmi out, Lakshmi in.
screen: `ALAKSHMI, SHOWN THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: A village before sunrise smells like several things at once. Woodsmoke. Wet earth. Milk warming in a pot. The cowshed, which nobody would call perfume. And then, from somewhere, a string of jasmine on a doorframe. Every one of those smells means the household is alive: fuel, food, animals fed, someone who cared enough to hang flowers. Today's lines of the Sri Sukta smell like that morning. The riches they name start in the cowshed and end in a person's mouth.
screen: `WOODSMOKE, WET EARTH, WARM MILK.` → `THE COWSHED, AND JASMINE.` → `A HOUSEHOLD THAT'S ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line, in paraphrase. Her doorway is fragrance. She is hard to overcome, always flourishing, rich in cow dung, the queen of all beings: I call Sri near. Yes, rich in cow dung. It's there in the Sanskrit, karishini, right next to queen of all beings, and the hymn sees no contradiction. In a farming household, dung is fuel for the fire, food for the fields and plaster for the floor. It means the cattle are healthy and the soil will feed you. So the goddess of fortune smells of jasmine at the door and of the cowshed out back, and both are signs of her. Now the next line. In paraphrase: may we gain the wish of the mind, the intention of the heart, the truth of speech. The beauty of cattle, and of food. May Sri and good name rest in me. First it asks for things nobody can store in a barn: an intention carried through, truth in what you say. In a hymn about fortune, truth of speech is counted as riches. And this is what Hindus mean when they say Lakshmi is more than money. A popular later hymn praises eight Lakshmis, the Ashta Lakshmi: wealth, yes, but also grain, courage, children, knowledge and victory among them. In village homes, cows are honored at Diwali, and floors are freshly plastered before the puja. The fortune this hymn wants is wider than a bank balance, and earthier, and it includes the way a person talks.
screen: `HER DOORWAY IS FRAGRANCE.` · `RICH IN COW DUNG, QUEEN OF ALL.` · `THE WISH, THE INTENTION, THE TRUTH.` · `EIGHT LAKSHMIS.` · then, large: `TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.`

segments.voice: Count your riches the way the eight Lakshmis do, one per breath: food today, a roof, someone who's family to you, a bit of courage, something you know, a small win. Then turn inward: an intention you've been carrying, something true you said this week, and let that count too. If you pray, you can give thanks to the goddess, or to God, for each; if you don't, let yourself be a little richer than you thought.

1099.title: Asking the Mud to Bring Her Home
1099.hook: a lotus pond drained in summer, all mud, and a hymn that asks the mud itself to bring the goddess home
1099.carry: the lotus: fortune rising clean from the mud
1099.tomorrow: what does a hymn of a thousand names call the goddess first?
1099.howItsDone: Some Hindus chant the whole Sri Sukta at home or in temples during Lakshmi worship, at Diwali and on other days, often while offering lotus flowers, lamps and sweets.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-NINETY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday counted truth of speech among its riches: Lakshmi is more than money. Today, she's asked to stay for good, and a week ends.
screen: `TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.`

segments.voice: Drain a lotus pond in the dry season and you don't find anything pretty. You find mud, thick and dark, with old roots running through it like cables. But that's where the flower lives. Every bloom draws on what's down there in the dark. The Sri Sukta has been calling the lotus goddess all week. And when it finally asks her to move in for good, it doesn't ask the flower to do the inviting. It asks the mud.
screen: `DRAIN THE POND. FIND MUD.` → `THAT'S WHERE THE FLOWER LIVES.` → `THE HYMN ASKS THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Through Kardama she has children. Kardama, come and dwell with me. Make Sri, the mother garlanded with lotuses, dwell in my family. Kardama is a name, and as a word it means mud. Tradition hears him as her son. So the singer asks her own child to move in, so his mother will follow. The next line does the same with water. In paraphrase: may the waters bring forth soft and gentle things. Chiklita, live in my house, and make the divine mother Sri dwell in my family. Chiklita, tradition says, is another of her children, linked to moisture. Mud and water: the two humble things a lotus can't live without. He doesn't ask the gold or the elephants to bring her, but the plainest, dampest parts of the earth. And this is why Lakshmi is called Padma and Kamala, both names for the lotus, and why she's pictured seated on one. Hindus love the lotus for what it does: it roots in mud and rises clean, water sliding off its leaves. Many teachers read it as a picture of a good life: grown out of ordinary, messy ground, and not stained by it. Notice the word family, too. Not my house only, but my people, across generations, some readers say. That's this week: a guest welcomed, a goddess who fills others, I choose you, a vow's heat, Alakshmi shown the door, riches wider than money, and now the mud. The hymn goes on a little further, but this is where the path leaves it. Tomorrow, a different hymn, one that praises the goddess by her names.
screen: `KARDAMA, WHOSE NAME MEANS MUD.` · `CHIKLITA, AND THE WATERS.` · `PADMA, KAMALA: THE LOTUS ONE.` · `DWELL IN MY FAMILY.` · then, large: `THE LOTUS RISES CLEAN FROM THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something plain that holds your life up: a hard season you came through, a parent's ordinary work, the early mornings. Then notice what has grown out of it that you're glad of now, and rest with the two together, root and flower. If you pray, you can thank the goddess, or God, for both; if you don't, let the plain thing be honored for once.
